entities.name: Periplus of the Erythraean Sea
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea is a seminal 1st-century Greco-Roman text that charted the coastline of the Indian Ocean and Red Sea. Created by an unknown author around 300 CE, this foundational work provides invaluable insights into the maritime trade networks of the ancient world.

The Periplus's significance lies in its meticulous descriptions of over 400 ports and settlements along the Erythraean coast, offering a unique window into the economic, cultural, and political dynamics of the region during the Roman Empire's peak. Notably, the text highlights the importance of the port city of Mocha (modern-day Yemen) as a major hub for trade between the East and West.

As a result of its detailed cartography, the Periplus has played a crucial role in shaping our understanding of ancient maritime commerce, influencing later works such as Ptolemy's Geography. Moreover, it has inspired numerous archaeological expeditions and continues to be an essential reference for scholars studying the history of navigation, trade, and cultural exchange in the ancient world.

Despite being over 1,800 years old, the Periplus remains a vibrant testament to human ingenuity, perseverance, and our enduring quest for knowledge and understanding.

In the words of historian and classicist, Edward Gibbon, 'The Erythraean Sea is a true marvel of ancient navigation, a testament to the ingenuity and skill of our ancestors.'
